197.title: Al-Fajr: the orphan, again
197.hook: no, you don't honor the orphan or urge feeding the poor, and you love wealth too much (89:17–20)
197.howItsDone: Caring for orphans is a long-standing Muslim practice: many sponsor an orphan through a charity, support orphanages, or take in relatives' children, recalling that the Prophet was himself an orphan.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Fajr's tour of the old cities, 'Ad, Thamud and Pharaoh. Your line was towers fall.

Listen to how people talk when life goes well. I worked hard. I earned this. Things are finally going my way. And when it goes badly: why me? What did I do to deserve this? Both sound natural. Both are about me. Al-Fajr catches that exact habit, reading every good day as a reward and every hard day as an insult, and then it does something sharp. It changes the subject to someone else entirely, someone this path has met twice already: the orphan.

Verses fifteen and sixteen show a person tested two ways. Given honor and comfort, he says: my Lord has honored me. Given a tight, narrow provision: my Lord has humiliated me. Then verse seventeen, in Pickthall's words: "Nay, but ye (for your part) honour not the orphan." The tables turn. You think the question is whether God honors you. The surah asks whether you honor the one with no one. Then three more. You don't urge each other to feed the poor. You swallow up inheritance, greedily; some commentators say this meant taking the shares of orphans and women, who couldn't defend them. And you love wealth with a love that has no bottom. This is the orphan's third visit on this stretch of the path. Ad-Duha: don't be harsh with the orphan. Al-Balad: feed an orphan who's a relative, on a day of hunger. Now here. And Ad-Duha tied the orphan to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ himself, in Pickthall's words: Did He not find thee an orphan? The biographies say his father died before he was born, and his mother while he was still small. A hadith in Bukhari says he held up two fingers, side by side, and said that he and the one who cares for an orphan will be in Paradise like this. Notice the verb, too. Not feed, or help. Honor, tukrimun, the same verb the man used about himself: my Lord has honored me. He wants honor; the surah asks him to give it. An orphan isn't a project. The surah asks for dignity, and asks you to urge others toward it, not only to give quietly yourself.

segments.voice: Think of a child who has lost a parent: one you know, a friend's child, a student, a neighbor, or one you'll never meet. Hold them in mind with respect, not pity. Then settle on one thing you could do: a gift to a charity that cares for orphans, a message to a grieving family, time with a child who needs a steady adult.

Your line: honor the orphan. Not only help the one with no one: honor. Day one hundred ninety-seven, done.

198.title: Al-Fajr: the soul at rest
198.hook: O soul at peace, return to your Lord, pleased and pleasing (89:27–30)
198.howItsDone: Muslims often speak of the nafs, the self, as moving between states, with the hope of one day being addressed as the soul at rest; the last verses of Al-Fajr are often recalled in times of loss.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Fajr, and the orphan, for the third time on this path. Your line was honor the orphan.

A key turns in the lock after a long trip. The smell of a familiar place, the bag dropped by the door, shoulders coming down an inch nobody knew they were up. That's rest: not only stopping, but arriving. Al-Fajr has been a hard surah. Old cities falling, the orphan neglected, then a scene of the Day itself, the earth ground to dust and people wishing they'd done more. Then, in its last four verses, the voice changes completely. It turns to one soul and speaks to it like someone coming home. Today: the soul at rest.
screen: `THE KEY IN THE LOCK.` → `NOT ONLY STOPPING. ARRIVING.` → `THE SOUL AT REST.`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-one: the earth ground down, flattened. Your Lord comes, and the angels, rank on rank. And the human being remembers, too late: if only I had sent something ahead for this life of mine. Then verse twenty-seven, in Pickthall's words: "But ah! thou soul at peace! Return unto thy Lord, content in His good pleasure!" Then: enter among My servants, enter My Garden. After all the thunder, the ending is spoken gently, to one soul. The Arabic is an-nafs al-mutma'innah. Mutma'innah means settled, at rest, reassured, the way water settles when you stop stirring it. It's the same root the Qur'an uses elsewhere: in the remembrance of God, hearts find rest. Later scholars, Ibn al-Qayyim among them, describe three states of the soul, drawn from three places in the Qur'an: the soul that pushes toward harm, from Surah twelve; the soul that blames itself, from Surah seventy-five; and this one, the soul at rest. Some read them not as three kinds of people, but as three states one person can move through, sometimes in a single afternoon. Then the last phrase: raadiyatan mardiyyah. Pleased, and pleasing. The soul is content with its Lord, and its Lord is content with it. It runs both ways. These verses are often recalled in grief, the picture of someone loved being called home. And the word is return. Not go somewhere strange. Go back to where you came from.

segments.voice: Don't try to be calm; just stop stirring, and let your shoulders come down the way they do when you get home. If thoughts swirl, let them, the way silt swirls before it sinks. At the end, notice whether anything settled, even a little.

199.title: Al-Ghashiyah: the overwhelming
199.hook: faces that day humbled, and faces that day joyful (88:1–16)
199.howItsDone: Following the Prophet's practice, imams often recite Al-Ghashiyah, with Al-A'la, in the Friday prayer and the prayers of the two Eids, so it is a surah often heard in congregation.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the end of Al-Fajr, the soul at rest called home. Your line was soul at rest, return.

A face gives the news before the mouth does. The doctor coming through the double doors. The teacher handing back the exam. A friend across the table who hasn't said a word yet. The story is already there, in the eyes and the set of the jaw. The surah before Al-Fajr tells the story of the Day through faces. Not scales or books, this time. Two kinds of faces, set side by side, and a question underneath simple enough to carry all day. Today: Al-Ghashiyah, the overwhelming.
screen: `THE NEWS IS IN THE FACE.` → `BEFORE A WORD IS SAID.` → `AL-GHASHIYAH, THE OVERWHELMING.`

segments.voice: Surah eighty-eight opens with a question, in Pickthall's words: Hath there come unto thee tidings of the Overwhelming? Al-ghashiyah comes from a root meaning to cover, to wrap completely, the way a wave covers a swimmer or a faint covers your senses. Commentators take it as a name for the Day of Judgment: the event that covers everything, that nobody can stand outside of. Then the faces. Some, that day, humbled, toiling, worn out; their work was hard and brought them nowhere. Others, that day, joyful, na'imah, soft with ease. And the next phrase is the surprise: pleased with their effort. The word for effort is sa'y, the same word met in Al-Layl ten days ago: your strivings differ. Both groups worked. Some commentators draw the lesson plainly: the difference wasn't effort; it was where the effort went, and what it was for. The joyful faces are placed in a lofty garden, with flowing springs, raised couches, cups set out, cushions lined up, carpets spread, like a host who has prepared everything before the guest arrives. A hadith in Muslim's collection says the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ recited it, together with Al-A'la, in the Friday prayer and the Eid prayers. So it's a surah often heard in a crowd, on a festival morning, surrounded by faces.

segments.voice: Notice your own face, the forehead, the jaw, the space between your eyebrows, and let anything clenched soften. Then think of one piece of work you're doing now, and picture looking back on it one day, your face open, pleased with the effort. What would have to be true of that work?
Al-Ghashiyah. The overwhelming, the Day that covers everything, and the name of Surah eighty-eight, told in faces. Today's word.

200.title: Al-Ghashiyah: look at the camel
200.hook: don't they look at the camel, the sky, the mountains, the earth spread out (88:17–20)
200.howItsDone: Muslims speak of tafakkur, reflective looking at creation, as a form of worship; the camel verses of Al-Ghashiyah are often quoted to invite it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Ghashiyah, the overwhelming, and the two kinds of faces. Your line was which face.

Day two hundred. That's a lot of mornings. So here's a question for this one: what did you see on your way here today? Not what was there. What did you see? It's easy to move through a day like a video playing with the sound off: trees, sky, a dog, a building, all of it wallpaper. Halfway through, Al-Ghashiyah does something unexpected. It stops talking about the next world and points at four very ordinary things in this one, starting with an animal its first listeners saw every day. Today: look at the camel.
screen: `WHAT DID YOU SEE TODAY?` → `THE WORLD AS WALLPAPER.` → `LOOK AT THE CAMEL.`

segments.voice: Verse seventeen, in Pickthall's words: Will they not regard the camels, how they are created? Then: and the sky, how it is raised. And the mountains, how they are set up. And the earth, how it is spread out. Picture the first listeners, in Mecca. Camels were part of daily life: transport, milk, wealth, the animal tied up outside the house. And the surah says: look at it. How was it made? An animal that crosses a desert carrying loads, going days without water. Then lift your eyes to the sky. Then the horizon, the mountains, fixed. Then down at your feet, ground spread flat enough to walk on and build on. Near, above, far, below: a full turn of the head. The argument is quiet. It doesn't list proofs. It asks you to pay attention, trusting that attention itself leads somewhere. Then verse twenty-one, a line for the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and for anyone who wants to share what they believe: so remind, for you are only a reminder. Verse twenty-two: you are not a controller over them. The word is musaytir, someone with authority to force. The Prophet's job, the surah says, was to point, like pointing at a camel: look. Not to make anyone see. Some readers take a rule of thumb from that line: the one who reminds is responsible for the reminding, not for what the other person does with it.
screen: `CAMEL, SKY, MOUNTAINS, EARTH.` · `AN EVERYDAY ANIMAL IN MECCA.` · `NEAR, ABOVE, FAR, BELOW.` · `A REMINDER, NOT A CONTROLLER.` · then, large: `LOOK AT THE CAMEL.`

segments.voice: Do the full turn of the head: first one thing near you, an object, a plant, your own hand, looked at as if you'd never seen one. Then the sky, or the ceiling if that's what's above you, then the farthest thing you can see, then the ground under you. Four things, looked at properly.
Al-Ghashiyah. The overwhelming, Surah eighty-eight, which pauses to say: look at the camel, the sky, the mountains, the earth. Today's word.

201.title: Al-A'la: the Most High
201.hook: glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High, who created and proportioned (87:1–3)
201.howItsDone: In every prostration of the prayer, Muslims say subhana rabbiyal a'la, glory to my Lord the Most High, usually three times, and in every bowing subhana rabbiyal 'azim; Al-A'la itself is often recited in the Friday, Eid and witr prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Ghashiyah, and four ordinary things worth a real look. Your line was look at the camel.

Watch Muslims pray, and there's one moment that stops people who've never seen it. The whole body goes down: knees, hands, and then forehead and nose on the floor. It's the lowest a human body can go while still awake. And if you could hear what's being said, quietly, into the carpet, you'd hear a phrase about height. Not about being low. About the Most High. That phrase comes straight from the opening line of the surah just before Al-Ghashiyah: Al-A'la, the Most High.
screen: `FOREHEAD ON THE FLOOR.` → `THE LOWEST A BODY CAN GO.` → `AL-A'LA, THE MOST HIGH.`

segments.voice: Surah eighty-seven opens, in Pickthall's words: Praise the name of thy Lord the Most High. The Arabic is sabbih: glorify, declare perfect. It's the root of subhanallah, glory be to God, a phrase this path met around day one hundred fourteen, counted thirty-three times on the fingers. And al-a'la, the Most High, from a root for height, being above. Then the surah says who this is: the one who created, then proportioned; who measured, then guided. Everything made, then balanced, then given a direction. Now the link to prayer. A hadith in Abu Dawud reports that when an earlier verse came, glorify the name of your Lord, the Magnificent, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said: put it in your bowing. And when this verse came, glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High, he said: put it in your prostration. So in the bowing, Muslims say subhana rabbiyal 'azim, glory to my Lord, the Magnificent. With the forehead on the ground, subhana rabbiyal a'la, glory to my Lord, the Most High. Usually three times, or more. At the exact moment the body is lowest, the words are about height. It isn't humiliation. It's perspective, like lying on your back under the night sky and suddenly knowing your size. Another hadith, in Muslim's collection, says the servant is closest to his Lord while in prostration. The lowest place, and the nearest.
screen: `SABBIH — GLORIFY, DECLARE PERFECT.` · `CREATED, PROPORTIONED, GUIDED.` · `PUT IT IN YOUR PROSTRATION.` · `THE LOWEST PLACE, AND THE NEAREST.` · then, large: `GLORY TO THE MOST HIGH.`

segments.voice: Let your body get a little lower than usual: sit on the floor if you can, or lower your head and let your shoulders drop, and feel the ground holding you while you think of the biggest thing you know, the sky, the ocean, the number of stars. If you pray, you can say quietly, three times: subhana rabbiyal a'la. If not, just rest in the feeling of your size.
Al-A'la. The Most High, the name of Surah eighty-seven, and the words Muslims say with their foreheads on the ground. Today's word.
Your line: glory to the most high. The good kind of small, the night-sky kind. That's day two hundred one.

202.title: Al-A'la: the one who purifies
202.hook: successful is the one who purifies, remembers and prays, though you prefer this life (87:14–17)
202.howItsDone: Muslims often recite Al-A'la in the Friday, Eid and witr prayers; its verses on the one who purifies himself and on the Hereafter being more lasting are often quoted in sermons and reminders.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-A'la, the Most High, and the words said with a forehead on the floor. Your line was glory to the most high.

A child at a kitchen table, one cookie on a plate. The deal: eat it now, or wait a little while and get two. Then the squirming starts. Eyes covered. Humming. A finger edging toward the plate. Grown-ups play the same game with money, sleep and phones, just less visibly. Now is loud. Later is quiet. Al-A'la names that pull. First it says who succeeds, and then, with an honesty that's almost tender, it admits what people actually prefer. Today: the one who purifies.
screen: `ONE COOKIE NOW, OR TWO LATER?` → `NOW IS LOUD. LATER IS QUIET.` → `THE ONE WHO PURIFIES.`

segments.voice: Verse fourteen: successful is the one who purifies himself. The verb is tazakka, from z-k-y, the root met ten days ago in Ash-Shams: successful is the one who purifies the soul. The same root as zakat: to cleanse, and to grow. Verse fifteen adds two more: he remembers the name of his Lord, and he prays. Purify, remember, pray. That's the whole description of success. Then verse sixteen turns to the listener, and doesn't scold. It just says: but you prefer the life of this world. It's true, and the surah knows it. Then verse seventeen, in Pickthall's words: "Although the Hereafter is better and more lasting." The key word is abqa, more lasting, from a root meaning to remain. It doesn't say this world is worthless. It says the later lasts longer. Verses eighteen and nineteen add a surprise: this is in the earlier scrolls, the scrolls of Ibrahim and Musa. Nothing new; Ibrahim and Musa were told the same. That closes a long stretch of the path. Since day one hundred seventy-seven, it has walked backward through the middle of the thirtieth part: the earthquake that reports, the clear proof, the Night of Power, the first word, read. The fig and the olive, the opened chest, the morning, the night, the sun and the soul, the steep path, the dawn, the overwhelming, and the Most High. Tomorrow come the opening surahs of the juz', still walking backward toward its first page.

segments.voice: Look at the choices ahead of you today: what you'll eat, what you'll watch, how you'll spend the evening, what you'll say to someone. Find one place where now and later pull in different directions. Don't solve them all; pick that one, and decide now which way it goes.
Al-A'la. The Most High, Surah eighty-seven: success is purifying, remembering, praying, and what comes later is more lasting. Today's word.
Your line: the later lasts. Purify, remember, pray. A whole stretch of the path, walked.

203.title: At-Tariq: the night star
203.hook: by the sky and the piercing star, every soul has a guardian over it (86:1–4)
203.howItsDone: At-Tariq is among the short surahs many Muslims memorize and recite in prayer; its verse on every soul having a guardian is often recalled as a comfort, and Muslims believe angels are assigned to watch over and record each person.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the end of Al-A'la, and of the middle surahs. Your line was the later lasts.

A knock on the door after midnight. The jolt, the heartbeat: who could that be? A knock at that hour usually means something. Arabic has a single word for that visitor, the one who comes knocking by night. And the surah just before Al-A'la uses it for something in the sky. A new stretch of the path starts here, the opening surahs of the thirtieth part, walked backward toward its first page. It starts with a knock. Today: At-Tariq, the night star.
screen: `A KNOCK AFTER MIDNIGHT.` → `THE ONE WHO COMES BY NIGHT.` → `AT-TARIQ, THE NIGHT STAR.`

segments.voice: Surah eighty-six begins: by the sky, and by at-tariq. The root t-r-q means to knock, to strike, and at-tariq is the one who comes knocking at night, a night visitor. Then the surah asks, as it often does: and what will make you know what at-tariq is? And answers: an-najm ath-thaqib, the piercing star, so bright it seems to punch a hole through the dark. Commentators have suggested different stars, and some say it means any bright star that appears at night. The text doesn't name one. Then the point the oaths were leading to, verse four, in Pickthall's words: No human soul but hath a guardian over it. The word is hafiz, one who keeps, protects and watches. Commentators explain it as the angels Muslims believe are assigned to each person, some protecting, some recording what they do. Others read it more broadly: God Himself keeps watch over every soul. Either way, the surah sets the two side by side. Up there in the dark, one bright point. Down here, over every single person, something keeping watch too. Not one soul is unattended. That ends a week: the orphan, again, then the soul at rest; the overwhelming, told in faces, and the camel worth a real look; the Most High, and the later that lasts. Now a star that knocks. The surah goes on to say that the human being was made from water poured out, and that the One who made him can bring him back. That waits for the path's later years.
screen: `AT-TARIQ — THE ONE WHO KNOCKS BY NIGHT.` · `THE PIERCING STAR.` · `HAFIZ — ONE WHO KEEPS AND WATCHES.` · `NOT ONE SOUL UNATTENDED.` · then, large: `EVERY SOUL HAS A GUARDIAN.`

segments.voice: Think of the people you love who are far from you tonight: a parent, a child, a friend in another city. Picture each one, one at a time, with a small bright point above them, keeping watch. Then picture one over yourself.
At-Tariq. The night visitor, the piercing star, and the name of Surah eighty-six: every soul has a guardian over it. Today's word.
Your line: every soul has a guardian. Up there one bright point; down here, a watch kept over everyone. Another week behind you.

the guardian set over every soul

myth: the Qur'an names which star at-tariq is
it calls it the piercing star; commentators suggest different stars, and the text leaves it open.
at-tariq comes from a root meaning to knock
the night visitor who comes knocking after dark.
commentators read the guardian only as God Himself
some say angels assigned to each person; others read it as God's own watch. both are held.

fork.setup: the surah swears by the sky and the night visitor, then asks: what will make you know what it is? what's the answer?
options: a traveler lost in the desert
fork.reveal: an-najm ath-thaqib, the piercing star (86:3): so bright it seems to punch a hole in the dark.

original.note: Arabic: the night visitor, from t-r-q, to knock or strike; the name of Surah 86.

trapdoor: what you thought: a surah about a star.
what it means: the bright star that comes at night stands beside a promise: no soul is without a guardian.

what a scholar hears: commentators note that tariq for a night visitor was ordinary Arabic; commentators link the guardian of 86:4 to the recording angels of 82:10–12 and the protecting angels of 13:11.

sources.ref: Qur'an 86:4
Qur'an 86:1–3 (the sky, the night visitor, the piercing star); 86:5–8 (made from gushing water; able to bring him back)
Qur'an 82:10–12; 13:11 (recording and protecting angels)
